label: Place
name: Democratic Republic of the Congo
summary:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), also known as Congo-Kinshasa, is the second-largest country in Africa by land area (2,344,858 km²) and the most populous Francophone country in the world (110 million people). Located in the heart of equatorial Africa, the DRC contains the world's second-largest tropical rainforest, the Congo Basin, which is one of the planet's most important carbon sinks and biodiversity reserves.

The Kongo Kingdom (14th–19th centuries) was one of the most sophisticated pre-colonial states in Central Africa. Belgian King Leopold II seized the Congo Free State as personal property in 1885 — a private colony of extraordinary brutality where rubber-collection quotas were enforced by mutilating workers who failed to meet them, killing an estimated 10 million people. Belgian formal colonization (1908–1960) continued exploitative extraction. Independence in June 1960 was followed within weeks by army mutiny, Katanga secession, and the assassination of Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba (1961) — orchestrated with CIA and Belgian involvement — marking the beginning of Cold War proxy conflict in Africa.

Mobutu Sese Seko's kleptocratic dictatorship (1965–1997) looted an estimated $5 billion from the country's mineral wealth. The First and Second Congo Wars (1996–2003) killed 5.4 million people — the deadliest conflict since World War II. The DRC's eastern provinces remain a theater of ongoing conflict over coltan, gold, and other minerals essential to global technology supply chains, making the DRC's instability a direct contributor to the electronics on which the digital world depends.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Belgian seizure of the Congo Free State led to an estimated 10 million deaths and brutal treatment of workers, making it a pivotal moment in African history and a warning against colonial exploitation. This event had significant regional impact on the development of Central Africa.
